💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 17:09 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 18:48 EST, 25 November 2026.
  • Andoni Iraola tried to stifle a smirk on Tuesday when it was put to him that he had a fair chance of completing a perfect week by thrashing Manchester United, winning away in Europe and then winning his first-ever Merseyside Derby.
  • The usual responses came back of remaining level-headed and not getting carried away, of course – but Iraola has ticked off two of those three tasks and now goes to Everton with his much-criticised, massive-money signings in the form of their Liverpool careers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS STEELE, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 17:09 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 18:48 EST, 25 November 2026.

Andoni Iraola tried to stifle a smirk on Tuesday when it was put to him that he had a fair chance of completing a perfect week by thrashing Manchester United, winning away in Europe and then winning his first-ever Merseyside Derby.

The usual responses came back of remaining level-headed and not getting carried away, of course – but Iraola has ticked off two of those three tasks and now goes to Everton with his much-criticised, massive-money signings in the form of their Liverpool careers.

That is Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz, of course, who both scored here to further quash any narratives over them being expensive flops, a debate which had followed them for much of their first year or so on Merseyside.

Isak scored a brace to take his season tally to double-figures and make it six away games in a row where he has struck, while Wirtz followed up his best performance of the season against United with a fine strike from distance.

Wirtz especially has never been far away from criticism during his time at the club but is silencing his doubters every week and remarked this week that Iraola had helped him rediscover the player Liverpool thought they were buying for £116million two summers ago.

In a recent development, the sentiment spreads beyond Wirtz. After a season of strife, Iraola has brought the feel-good factor back at Anfield and supporters are enjoying watching their team again after a year in which it felt like a chore to do so some weeks.

Alexander Isak scored twice as Liverpool beat Club Brugge 3-0 in the Champions League.

That made it three wins in a row for the Reds as they start to really click under Andoni Iraola.

CLUB BRUGGE (4-3-3): Sommer 4; Sabbe 5 (Siquet 84), Spileers 5, Mechele 6, Seys 6; Vetlesen 6 (Vermant 75), Potts 7 (Tsawa 84), Vanaken 6; Forbs 7, Tresoldi 6, Lemarechal 7 (Diakhon 75).

Subs not used: Jackers, Vanden Driessche, Han-beom Lee, Virgili, Dams, Robberechts, Audoor, Vasovic.

LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1): Alisson 7; Frimpong 6 (Van Dijk 73, 6), Araujo 6, Jacquet 7, Kerkez 6; Nyoni 7 (Mac Allister 73, 6), Szoboszlai 7; Munoz 6 (Ngumoha 42, 6), Wirtz 7, Barcola 6 (Chambers 86); ISAK 8 (Koumas 86).

Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Tsimikas, McConnell, Danns.

Scorers: Isak 13, 82, Wirtz 79.

Referee: Alejandro Hernandez (Esp) 6.

It is making the Liverpool fans fall for Iraola a little bit more each week. How that feeling would be turbocharged with Derby delight at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Sunday.

In a recent development, ‘I was very pleased with the result and the performance overall,’ noted Iraola. ‘At 3-0, you can think it was an easy game and I don’t think it was. We were facing a really good team.’.

As the 1,000 or so travelling Kop enjoyed their strong Belgian beers and chocolate waffles in this quaint, picturesque city, they were still laughing about poor old Manchester United and Sunday’s 4-0 demolition job.

This was a much tougher test against an opposition that had started well in the Champions League with three wins from four, so Liverpool’s performance was never going to be as convincing – but the victory was still vital.

It helped them take a step closer to cementing a top eight place in this long-winded league phase. That would ease the pressure on a congested calendar by seeing them not only be able to rest players in the latter games of the league stage but also skip a play-off round.

Club Brugge are no mugs and they showed that, with energetic winger Carlos Forbs the pick of the bunch. The former Manchester City academy starlet has inherited a certain Cristiano Ronaldo’s No 7 shirt at Portugal and gave Milos Kerkez a testing night here.

Sources indicate that the Belgian side, like Liverpool, had won three of their first four European games including victory away to Inter. They had won five of the last seven league titles with a brave playing style that Iraola admitted was a pleasure to analyse – which he added was not always the case.

Industry observers note that their bold approach was their undoing here, though, with possession tossed away far too easily for Liverpool’s opener after 13 minutes. Yann Sommer, in the winter of his career at 37, passed straight to Bradley Barcola who, via stand-in skipper Dominik Szoboszlai, found Isak.

The Swede needed no second invitation to fire home his ninth goal of the season. Isak had been rested for most of Liverpool’s early European outings but was the difference here and loves playing away: he has now netted on his last six games away from Anfield.

Liverpool have 12 points from five games and will almost certainly be in the knockout stages.

Florian Wirtz continued his fine form as he curled in a delightful effort to put Liverpool 2-0 up.

Iraola will hope to make it the perfect week with victory in Sunday's Merseyside Derby.

Sources indicate that only Mohamed Salah has done so in seven or more in recent history for Liverpool. Everton would be a fine place to match that record.

In a recent development, despite the scoreline flattering Liverpool, things were far from easy after Isak’s opener. Alisson was needed to deny Felix Lemarechal both sides at half-time and Virgil van Dijk – rested from the start – was called on as a second-half substitute to steady the ship.

Winger Victor Munoz limped off in agony after going down before half-time holding his knee. Iraola feared the worst when a stretcher was called but the Spaniard walked off and was feeling ‘optimistic’ after the match, according to the boss.

Szoboszlai should have put the game to bed after a sublime team move led to the Hungarian being thwarted by Sommer at point-blank range, while Barcola was also guilty of wastefulness after getting his feet tangled up when in a dangerous position.

But Wirtz, in the best form of his Liverpool career, made it three goals in his last three with a fine strike from distance that clipped in off the post.

Then Isak raced through on goal and dinked a shot over Sommer for goal No 10 of the season for him. It completed a memorable night for Iraola and his major-money boys. Now to make it a perfect week at Everton on Sunday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unconvincing Celtic kept their Europa League qualification hopes alive with a hard-fought and historic 2-1 victory over Portuguese second-tier side Torreense.

Martin O’Neill’s men took an early lead through a Javi Vazquez own goal after nine minutes, but Dany Jean restored parity for the hosts before half-time in Leiria.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The visitors struggled to find a breakthrough after the interval, until substitute Camilo Duran rose unmarked to head home James Forrest’s cross in the 84th minute.

The late winner secured a second consecutive victory in the competition for Celtic, moving them on to six points from five matches and up to 25th in the league-phase standings after keeping their hopes of reaching the knockout stages alive.

It was also the Scottish champions’ victory win on Portuguese soil since 2003.

Lewis Anderson watched the action unfold for The Scotsman and picks out his four main takeaways from the game.

Celtic may have made unnecessarily hard work of beating a Portuguese second division outfit at the moment sitting 13th in their league, but Martin O’Neill will care little about the aesthetics after securing three precious points.

Industry observers note that although Celtic enjoyed plenty of possession after the interval, their use of the ball was frequently pedestrian, with too many passes going sideways or backwards rather than putting Torreense under meaningful pressure. There were spells when Celtic appeared destined to settle for a frustrating draw, but ultimately they have given themselves a genuine opportunity to reach the play-off round and, at this stage of their European campaign, that is what matters most.

Once again, Camilo Duran proved to be the difference-maker. O’Neill's decision to keep the in-form striker in reserve paid dividends, with the substitute delivering the decisive moment when Celtic needed a spark. The Colombian’s back-post header from fellow replacement James Forrest’s pinpoint delivery was precisely the injection of quality that had been missing for much of the evening.

According to recent reports, when the ball arrived at his feet, his first touch was outstanding, allowing him to open his body and switch the play. He then demonstrated the instincts of a natural goal scorer, occupying defenders before finding the space to deliver the decisive finish. Duran may have had only 12 touches, but the one that mattered most was emphatic. He is becoming Celtic's go-to man in crucial moments, and delivered once more when it counted.

Recent findings suggest that although Jota did not manage to get his name on the scoresheet or provide an assist, his performance in Portugal offered plenty of telltale signs that he is rediscovering the devastating form that once made him such an exciting attacking presence for Celtic. The winger looked particularly at home on his return to familiar surroundings, relishing the chance to perform in front of friends and family after an arduous period on the sidelines.

In a recent development, making his first European appearance since Celtic’s Champions League disappointment against Bayern Munich in February 2025, the 27-year-old showed few signs of rustiness despite two injury-disrupted seasons. He was a constant menace to Torreense down the left flank, using his pace, close control and willingness to take on defenders to cause problems throughout his time on the pitch.

His influence was particularly evident during the opening period, creating two opportunities, testing the goalkeeper twice and delivering a succession of enticing crosses that deserved more decisive finishing from his team-mates. One such delivery contributed to Celtic's opening goal, when Vazquez inadvertently turned the ball into his own net.

Recent findings suggest that given the length of his absence and the physical demands of returning to elite-level football, there had been understandable questions over whether Jota could recapture the explosive qualities that previously made him a favourite among the Celtic support. His latest display provided a really encouraging response. There is still work to do before he reaches his previous heights, but the signs are increasingly promising.

It has been revealed that this success has breathed fresh life into Celtic's European campaign, but O’Neill will be under no illusions that there is considerable scope for improvement if his side are to make further progress. Individual contributions may have rescued the evening in Portugal, yet they should not disguise some worrying collective shortcomings, particularly the vulnerability of the defence and the lack of composure when chances presented themselves in the final third.

The format offers Celtic a route into the knockout stages, with the top eight in the league phase advancing automatically to the last 16, while those finishing between ninth and 24th must negotiate a two-legged play-off. There remains little margin for error, though, with three fixtures remaining. Celtic still have Omonoia, Marseille and current league-phase leaders Union Saint-Gilloise to negotiate, and will almost certainly require further points if they are to extend their European journey.

There is, however, reason for optimism. The win over Torreense means Celtic have now recorded successive wins in a major European competition for the first time since defeating Ferencvaros home and away during the 2021-22 group stage of this tournament. It is a positive milestone for O’Neill's side and another indication that, despite their problems, Celtic are beginning to build some momentum at a crucial stage.

In a recent development, torreense may have been unfancied on paper, but they demonstrated they were no pushovers and gave Celtic a considerably sterner test than their second-tier status might have suggested. The Portuguese outfit were organised, and disciplined, refusing to be overawed by the occasion or the gulf in resources between the two clubs.

João Nuno’s side pressed aggressively, competed well for second balls and revealed enough attacking ambition to expose some of Celtic's defensive vulnerabilities. Their equaliser was reward for an approach that refused to crumble after falling behind, while their resistance after the interval threatened to frustrate the visitors further.

According to recent reports, celtic's superior individual quality eventually told, but Torreense deserve credit for making them dig deep for the result. This was no routine European assignment. For all the criticism Celtic will face over aspects of their performance, Torreense should not be dismissed as cannon fodder. They showed spirit and sufficient quality to suggest their lowly league position told only part of the story.

#152428. Breaking: Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.
  • The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.
  • Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care. In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Industry observers note that half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

Industry observers note that in the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Recent findings suggest that exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a fresh cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that for people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

According to recent reports, in another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she noted. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

According to recent reports, nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell remarked that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she stated.

According to recent reports, nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he stated.

In a recent development, he is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

Recent findings suggest that in a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

Recent findings suggest that "There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together.".

Recent findings suggest that campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she noted, if run by properly trained staff.

According to recent reports, one recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she noted.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

It has been revealed that according to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he mentioned.

By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 16:19, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 10:30.

Manchester United, Arsenal and Chelsea have reportedly suffered a major blow in their pursuits of Barcelona star Fermin Lopez.

Mauricio Pochettino's Red Devils are at the moment occupying 19th position in the Premier League standings after their worst-ever start to the competition, picking up just the single top-flight victory to date.

Following a defeat by Liverpool at Anfield last weekend, Man Utd managed to record a 2-2 Champions League draw at Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday night, when the visitors were arguably unlucky to miss out on maximum points.

On the fringes of Michael Carrick's and now Pochettino's looks at Old Trafford, Marcus Rashford could supposedly move away from the club during the January transfer window if a suitable offer arrives.

Elsewhere in attack, Bruno Fernandes has been the club's best player since the start of the decade; however, the Portugal international could be on his way out of Man Utd next summer.

According to TEAMtalk, Premier League giants Manchester United, Arsenal and Chelsea all made enquiries for Barcelona's Lopez during the recent summer transfer window, with the Spanish side snubbing those advances.

The 23-year-old put pen to paper on a fresh deal at the beginning of this calendar year and it is understood that the attacker has commenced talks with the Catalan club over another contract extension.

With the player's current deal expiring in June 2031, Barca are in no danger of losing Lopez on the cheap anytime soon; however, Hansi Flick's side are keen to reward the Spaniard further for an exceptional start to the 2026-27 campaign.

The former Linares Deportivo loanee has become such an integral figure at Camp Nou that the interested Premier League trio have supposedly been told to 'forget about' their dreams of signing the forward.

The future of Fernandes at Man Utd is unclear heading towards his contract expiration in June, with the Red Devils reportedly highlighting Barca's Lopez as a potential successor to the Portuguese's Old Trafford spot.

Yet to reach top form, Lopez was not a guaranteed starter for Flick's Barcelona last season - a situation that allowed Manchester United, Arsenal and Chelsea to dream of signing the talent.

However, the picture surrounding the 23-year-old has changed dramatically this campaign, with the 12-time international starting 10 La Liga matches already, cementing a spot in the XI behind the lone striker.

In all competitions, Lopez has netted nine times and provided seven assists across 17 appearances, with only Lamine Yamal and Raphinha notching up more goal contributions for Barca in La Liga.

#152424. Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation

Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 95 min read (18959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~95 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that cancer-associated mutations in PIK3CA underlie congenital overgrowth disorders that frequently involve the vasculature1,2.
  • Somatic and germline pathogenic variants in cancer-associated genes cause diverse congenital disorders1,2 and are also found in phenotypically normal tissue4,5.
  • Recent findings suggest that PIK3CA encodes p110α, the catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3Kα), which regulates cell growth, proliferation, migration and metabolism6 through AKT and downstream effectors, including mTOR and forkhead box O (FOXO) transcription factors7,8.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cancer-associated mutations in PIK3CA underlie congenital overgrowth disorders that frequently involve the vasculature1,2. Among the affected tissues, the endothelium commonly exhibits aberrant expansion, leading to vascular malformations3. Notably, these lesions arise predominantly in veins and capillaries, whereas arteries are largely spared, for reasons that remain unclear. Here, using genetic lineage tracing, we show that endothelial expression of PIK3CAH1047R drives profound clonal expansion of capillary and venous endothelial cells, whereas mature arterial endothelial cells are refractory to pathological PI3K activation. Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features, providing a mechanistic explanation for the paucity of arterial lesions after PIK3CA genetic perturbation. Mechanistically, these effects are mediated by two complementary downstream branches of PI3K signalling: increased proliferation, which drives vascular overgrowth, and upregulation of the venous-specifying transcription factor NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), which suppresses arterial differentiation. Together, our findings reveal that pathogenic responses to PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial differentiation state and fate trajectory, and demonstrate that arterial endothelium is intrinsically resistant to oncogenic PI3K signalling. Arteries are therefore shielded from PIK3CA mutations, explaining the rarity of arterial malformations in PIK3CA-driven disease.

Somatic and germline pathogenic variants in cancer-associated genes cause diverse congenital disorders1,2 and are also found in phenotypically normal tissue4,5. Germline mutations may be inherited or arise de novo, whereas somatic mutations, acquired during embryonic development, generate mosaicism and a broad spectrum of phenotypes1. Understanding how identical mutations produce distinct outcomes across tissues is crucial for defining cellular susceptibility to disease and explaining the phenotypic heterogeneity.

Recent findings suggest that PIK3CA encodes p110α, the catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3Kα), which regulates cell growth, proliferation, migration and metabolism6 through AKT and downstream effectors, including mTOR and forkhead box O (FOXO) transcription factors7,8. PIK3CA is an oncogene that is frequently mutated in both mosaic congenital disorders9 and phenotypically normal tissue4. Activating mutations occur throughout the coding sequence, with recurrent hotspots including E545K, E542K, H1047R and H1047L3. Mesoderm-derived tissues, including the endothelium, are commonly affected in PIK3CA-related congenital disorders, which manifest as aberrant tissue overgrowth and vascular malformations10,11,12,13. Although PIK3CA mutations have been extensively studied in adult epithelial tissues14,15,16,17, their effects on cellular heterogeneity, differentiation and clonal dynamics in mesoderm-derived lineages remain poorly understood.

Recent findings suggest that vascular malformations are congenital vascular anomalies classified as slow-flow lesions, affecting capillaries, veins and lymphatic vessels or fast-flow lesions, often involving arteries18. Somatic activating PIK3CA mutations occur in the endothelium of all major slow-flow vascular malformations, where lesion expansion requires mitogenic signals, even though the mutation alone is insufficient to confer a proliferative advantage19,20,21,22. By contrast, no evidence presently implicates PIK3CA mutations in fast-flow arterial malformations3. Whether arterial endothelial cells have these mutations but resist their effects, or mutant clones are negatively selected or eliminated in arterial vessels remains unclear.

Here we demonstrate that endothelial responses to oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R are governed by cellular identity and developmental trajectory. Combining mosaic genetics, lineage tracing and single-cell analyses, we identify a differentiation-stage-specific window of susceptibility to pathological PI3K signalling, while fully differentiated arterial endothelial cells are resistant. These findings provide a framework for the tissue and vessel-type specificity of PIK3CA-driven vascular malformations.

Postnatal expression of Pik3caH1047R (Pik3catm1.1Waph/+) from the endogenous locus in mouse retinal endothelial cells using Pdgfb-creERT2 results in venous and capillary malformations, whereas arteries remain unaffected19 (Extended Data Fig. 1a–e). To correlate these phenotypes with the distribution of mutant cells, we introduced the R26-mTmG reporter allele into the Pik3caH1047RPdgfb-creERT2 mice (pan-endothelial (pEC)-GFP-Pik3caH1047R; Fig. 1a). Tamoxifen-mediated Cre activation induced recombination of the endogenous Pik3caH1047R allele and the reporter, resulting in membrane-bound GFP expression that marks recombined cells and therefore approximates Pik3caH1047R-expressing endothelial cells. Pdgfb-creERT2R26-mTmG mice were used as controls (pEC-GFP). After low-dose administration of 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) at postnatal day 1 (P1), retinas were analysed at P6 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). Mosaic recombination was observed throughout the vascular plexus in both genotypes (Fig. 1b). Although GFP+ mutant cells were present in all vessel types, vascular malformations occurred exclusively in capillaries and veins (Fig. 1c,d). In these vessels, mutant GFP+ endothelial cells underwent marked clonal expansion, generating enlarged vascular tubes (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1f), accompanied by increased endothelial cell proliferation during early lesion formation (Extended Data Fig. 1g–i). By contrast, Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells in arteries neither expanded nor altered vessel width (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1f). Consistent with these phenotypes, capillary and venous mutant GFP+ cells displayed increased PI3K pathway activation, as assessed by staining of phosphorylated S6 (p-S6), whereas arterial mutant cells revealed no detectable increase relative to wild-type (WT) cells (Fig. 1d,f). These data show that Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells selectively expand in capillaries and veins, while arteries remain structurally and molecularly normal despite containing mutant cells.

Recent findings suggest that a, Schematic of the transgenic strategy and endothelial populations targeted by low-dose 4-OHT-induced Pdgfb-creERT2 activation; pEC, pan-endothelial cells. b, Confocal images of P6 retinas stained for IB4 (red, blood vessels) and GFP (cyan/grey, Pdgfb-targeted endothelial cells). c, The incidence of vascular malformations in P6 pEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas (n = 8 retinas). d, High-magnification confocal images of P6 retinas stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and p-S6 (Ser235/236) (yellow/grey, PI3K readout). The white dotted rectangles indicate the regions magnified on the right. e,f, Quantification of GFP+ area (n = 13, 19, 5, 15, 5 and 13 retinas, left to right) (e) and p-S6 fluorescence within GFP+ areas (n = 6, 8, 5, 8, 5 and 7 retinas, left to right) (f) in capillaries, veins and arteries. g, Schematic of the transgenic strategy and endothelial population targeted by 4-OHT-induced Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 activation. aEC, arterial endothelial cells. h,i, Confocal images of P9 aEC-GFP and aEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red) and GFP (cyan, Bmx-targeted endothelial cells) (h) or IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and p-S6 (grey) (i). j,k, GFP+ arterial area (n = 6 and 11 retinas, left to right) (j) and p-S6 fluorescence within GFP+ areas (n = 6 and 7 retinas, left to right) (k). Data are mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (e,f,j,k). Scale bars, 150 μm (b,h) and 30 μm (d,i). FC, fold change; NS, not significant.

It has been revealed that the apparent resistance of arterial endothelial cells to Pik3caH1047R prompted us to directly investigate the behaviour of mutant cells in arteries. To this end, we used the Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 mouse line, which specifically targets arterial endothelial cells in retinal vessels. WT and Pik3caH1047R arterial endothelial cells (aEC) were traced by combining Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 and R26-mTmG with or without the Pik3caH1047R allele (aEC-GFP and aEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R; Fig. 1g). Bmx(PAC)-creERT2-mediated tracing revealed robust arterial recombination after 4-OHT administration at P4 or P7, whereas induction at P1 did not label arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). Thus, recombination was induced at P4 or P7 for subsequent experiments. In both settings, the proportion of GFP+ cells and arterial vessel width were comparable between the mutant and control retinas (Fig. 1h–j and Extended Data Fig. 2c–f). Arteries also displayed similar smooth-muscle-cell coverage and maintained expression of arterial markers UNC5B and CX37 (Extended Data Fig. 2g–j). Moreover, GFP+ arterial endothelial cells of both genotypes lacked expression of NR2F2, a key transcription factor that suppresses arterial identity23,24,25,26 (Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). Consistent with earlier observations, mutant GFP+ cells indicated low PI3K pathway activation, with no increase relative to controls (Fig. 1i,k and Extended Data Fig. 2m,n). To assess the long-term effects, we analysed retinas at P21. No differences were detected in the GFP+ cell distribution, arterial morphology or NR2F2 expression between WT and Pik3caH1047R cells in main arteries and arteriolar branches (Extended Data Fig. 2o–q). These findings show that mutant cells persist in arteries or arteriolar branches without detectable changes in arterial identity, morphology or PI3K activation, supporting the resistance of differentiated arterial endothelial cells to Pik3caH1047R.

To investigate why arterial endothelial cells are protected against Pik3caH1047R, we pharmacologically disrupted key arterial features in aEC-GFP and aEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R pups. As arterial endothelial cells experience higher shear stress, we first reduced systemic blood pressure with the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor captopril27. Although captopril reduced KLF4 expression and induced dilation of the vascular plexus28, it did not alter the proportion of GFP+ cells or arterial width. Furthermore, endothelial proliferation was not increased in mutant arteries (Extended Data Fig. 3a–d). We next inhibited Notch signalling, a key regulator of arterial differentiation and maintenance, using N-[N-(3,5-difluorophenacetyl)-l-alanyl]-S-phenylglycine t-butyl ester (DAPT). Despite a pronounced response in sprouting capillaries, DAPT likewise did not elicit any response in arteries to Pik3caH1047R expression (Extended Data Fig. 3a,e,f). Collectively, these results indicate that inhibition of major arterial identity programmes alone is insufficient to overcome arterial resistance to Pik3caH1047R.

To test whether resistance to Pik3caH1047R emerges during arterial differentiation, we traced tip endothelial cells—a pre-arterial population that contributes to arterial growth29,30. We used the Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 mouse line, which specifically marks tip cells, crossed with R26-mTmG (tEC-GFP) alone or in combination with Pik3caH1047R (tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R; Fig. 2a). 4-OHT was administered at P1, and Esm1-GFP+ progeny were analysed at different timepoints (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Then, 24 h after induction, GFP+ cells were predominantly localized at the sprouting front (Fig. 2b). By P6, GFP+ cells contributed extensively to arteries in tEC-GFP retinas, and the GFP+ arterial area further increased by P8 (Fig. 2b). Consistent with previous reports30, a subset of Esm1-traced cells also contributed to the capillary plexus (Fig. 2b). Pik3caH1047R expression markedly reduced the GFP+ area within arteries (Fig. 2b–f and Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). Instead, most mutant GFP+ cells were retained in the capillary bed, where they expanded (Fig. 2d,f and Extended Data Fig. 4b–f) and formed multiple vascular malformations (Fig. 2b,c). Moreover, mutant, but not control, GFP+ cells were frequently detected in veins (Fig. 2b–f and Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). The few Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells that reached arteries did not induce pathology (Fig. 2c). Consistent with lesion formation, Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells displayed increased p-S6 levels in capillaries, but not in arteries (Fig. 2e,g and Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). By P21, Pik3caH1047R GFP+ clones persisted in capillaries and veins, although they did not further expand (Extended Data Fig. 4i–l). These data indicate that Pik3caH1047R expression impairs mobilization of arterial precursors to arteries, resulting in their retention within capillaries and the diversion of a subset towards veins, where they expand and form vascular malformations.

Representative of ten retinas across three independent experiments. c, The incidence of vascular malformations in P6 tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas (n = 6 retinas). d,e, High-magnification confocal images of P8 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red) and GFP (cyan) (d) or IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and p-S6 (Ser235/236, yellow/grey) (e). f, GFP+ endothelial area in capillaries, veins and arteries. n = 8 retinas per genotype. g, p-S6 fluorescence within GFP+ capillaries (n = 7 and 8 retinas, left to right) and arterial areas (n = 7 and 5 retinas, left to right). h, Schematic of the transgenic strategy and targeted endothelial population. Yellow and blue nuclei indicate mutant and WT cells, respectively. i, Confocal images of P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (magenta), Cherry (cyan, WT) and eGFP (yellow, PIK3CAH1047R-expressing cells). A, artery; V, vein. The cyan arrows indicate WT cells. Representative of 30 retinas across 10 independent experiments. j, The distribution of recombined Cherry+ and eGFP+ Esm1-derived progeny within arteries and capillaries/veins at P8. The numbers indicate cell counts and percentages. n = 6 retinas. k, High-magnification confocal images of P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas. The arrow indicates an arterial lesion. l,m, The percentage of Ki-67+ cells (n = 6 retinas) (l) and p-S6 fluorescence (n = 4 retinas) (m) in Cherry+ and eGFP+ capillary endothelial cells. n, Arteries containing Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells among arteries containing recombined endothelial cells (n = 14 retinas). Data are mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (f,g,l,m). Scale bars, 150 μm (b,i) and 30 μm (d,e,k).

To directly compare WT and mutant endothelial cells within the same tissue, we generated a multispectral genetic mouse model, termed iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R). Cre-mediated recombination stochastically generates either His-H2B-Cherry (WT) or H2B-eGFP-V5 together with HA-PIK3CAH1047R (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Validation in primary endothelial cells confirmed preferential generation of Cherry+ cells, as reported for related constructs31, and increased proliferation and PI3K pathway activation in eGFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 5b–h). To fate-map pre-arterial endothelial cells in vivo, we crossed iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice with Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 mice (tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R) (Fig. 2h). As the recombination efficiency was lower than in Pik3catm1.1Waph/+ mice, we increased the 4-OHT dose, and retinas were analysed 7 days after induction (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Cherry+ cells contributed to both capillaries and arteries (Fig. 2i–k). By contrast, eGFP+ cells were predominantly located in capillaries, including those adjacent to arteries, and in veins, where they expanded and formed vascular malformations (Fig. 2i–k and Extended Data Fig. 6b). eGFP+ cells greatly outnumbered Cherry+ cells (7,680 versus 511) and displayed increased Ki-67 positivity and p-S6 levels (Fig. 2j,l,m and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). Despite their expansion, only 0.47% of total eGFP+ cells was incorporated into arteries, compared with 23% of Cherry+ cells (Fig. 2j). Overall, mutant endothelial cells were detected in only 16% of arteries containing recombined cells (Fig. 2n). Co-staining for eGFP, Cherry and ERG confirmed that lesions consisted exclusively of mutant cells (Extended Data Fig. 6e).

According to recent reports, in contrast to Esm1+ cells expressing Pik3caH1047R from the endogenous locus, which did not induce arterial pathology (Fig. 2c,e), all eGFP+ cells that reached arteries in the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model formed small lesions (averaging nine cells per lesion) (Fig. 2k). We therefore tested whether forced overexpression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial endothelial cells would produce a similar phenotype. To this end, we combined iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R with Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 and induced recombination between P4 and P6, or between P7 and P9 (Extended Data Fig. 6f–i). Five days later, the expected proportions of Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells were detected (Extended Data Fig. 6h). Mutant arterial cells remained non-pathogenic after late recombination; however, targeting at P4–6 resulted in mild arterial overgrowth in around 20% of arteries containing recombined mutant cells (Extended Data Fig. 6f–i). Across models, arterial width inversely correlated with endothelial differentiation state at the time of PIK3CAH1047R expression (Extended Data Fig. 6i). eGFP+ arterial endothelial cells showed increased PI3K signalling activation compared with neighbouring Cherry+ cells under all conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6g,j). By contrast, endogenous Pik3caH1047R expression did not increase arterial p-S6 levels (Figs. 1d,f,i,k and 2e,g). Nonetheless, eGFP+ arterial cells still lacked NR2F2 expression (Extended Data Fig. 6k), consistent with maintained arterial identity. Together, these data indicate that arterial resistance to PIK3CAH1047R depends on endothelial differentiation state and mutant expression level. Forced overexpression partially overcomes this resistance at earlier developmental stages, promoting mild arterial overgrowth without inducing NR2F2 expression.

Sources indicate that to investigate how Pik3caH1047R impairs arterial mobilization, we analysed endothelial cell transcriptomes using single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. We profiled endothelial cells from tEC-GFP (6,564 cells) and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R (19,168 cells) retinas, enabling molecular tracing of Esm1+ tip cells and their progeny (Fig. 3a). We first defined endothelial transcriptional states in WT retinas by clustering scRNA-seq data from tEC-GFP retinas. Unsupervised analysis identified nine populations: tip, pre-arterial angiogenic, metabolic angiogenic, proliferative 1, proliferative 2, venous, capillary, arterial capillary and arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7a–c and Supplementary Data 1). Notably, hierarchical clustering based on average gene expression profiles grouped tip, proliferative and metabolic angiogenic populations together, whereas pre-arterial angiogenic endothelial cells were more similar to arterial and arterial-capillary populations, supporting their arterial bias (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Traced cells were identified by GFP transcripts (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Projection of GFP expression onto the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) revealed Esm1-traced cells in all clusters except for the venous population (Extended Data Fig. 7f–h). Approximately half of Esm1-traced cells localized to arterial populations, whereas around 20% remained proliferative, indicating that Esm1-derived endothelial cells normally retain proliferative capacity while progressively differentiating into the arterial lineage (Extended Data Fig. 7h).

According to recent reports, we next examined whether Pik3caH1047R affects this developmental trajectory. To address this, we jointly analysed WT and Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells. Integrated analysis resolved seven endothelial populations: tip (C1), metabolic angiogenic (C2), proliferative 1 (C3), proliferative 2 (C4), venous (C5), arterial capillary (C6) and arterial (C7) endothelial cells (Fig. 3b,c, Extended Data Fig. 7i and Supplementary Data 1). GFP expression revealed a marked redistribution of Esm1-traced cells (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7j,k). Whereas WT GFP+ cells predominantly localized to arterial capillary and arterial clusters (C6 and C7), Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells were instead enriched within angiogenic, proliferative and venous clusters (C2, C3, C4 and C5) (Fig. 3d,e and Extended Data Fig. 7k). Quantification confirmed selective expansion of mutant GFP+ cells in proliferative, angiogenic and venous clusters, but not arterial clusters (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 7k). Importantly, Pik3ca expression was comparable across all endothelial clusters (Extended Data Fig. 7l).

Industry observers note that to determine whether this redistribution also reflected altered endothelial transcriptional identity, we performed cluster-specific differential expression analysis comparing GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial populations. We identified transcriptional alterations between WT and mutant cells in all clusters, with only limited changes in arterial cells (C7), consistent with the resistance observed in differentiated arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7m). The tip cluster (C1) contained too few cells for robust differential expression analysis (Extended Data Fig. 7k). Affected clusters demonstrated a consistent shift towards venous-associated gene expression, accompanied by reduced tip, arterial, guidance and capillary-specialization programmes (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 7n). This pattern remained after correcting for differences in cluster size (Supplementary Fig. 1). Hierarchical clustering further showed the greatest genotype-dependent divergence in angiogenic and venous populations (Extended Data Fig. 7o). We next performed RNA velocity analysis on subclustered GFP+ cells, which revealed altered cell-state dynamics in Esm1-traced mutant endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7p,q and Supplementary Data 1). Whereas WT GFP+ cells displayed coherent trajectories toward capillary and arterial states, mutant cells showed altered cell-state trajectories, with prominent progression toward proliferative and venous-associated populations and reduced progression toward the arterial lineage (Extended Data Fig. 7r). Together, these findings indicate that Pik3caH1047R promotes endothelial proliferation while diverting differentiating endothelial cells away from the arterial programme towards venous-associated cell states.

To determine whether this programme is initiated rapidly after Pik3caH1047R expression, we analysed cultured sister endothelial cells derived from Pik3caH1047RPdgfb-creERT2 mice using scRNA-seq (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b and Supplementary Data 2). Endothelial identity across clusters was confirmed by uniform Pecam1 expression, and Pik3ca expression was comparable between clusters (Extended Data Fig. 8c,d). Acute Pik3caH1047R expression recapitulated the in vivo transcriptional changes, with expansion of proliferative and venous-like populations and reduction of tip/arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 8e–g). Mutant cells also expressed higher levels of venous markers (that is, Nr2f2 and Nrp2) and lower levels of tip markers (that is, Esm1 and Angpt2) (Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). These data indicate that Pik3caH1047R rapidly and cell-autonomously initiates a programme of proliferation and loss of arterial identity.

According to recent reports, we next examined how this transcriptional transition unfolds during arterial differentiation in vivo by staining tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas at P4 and P6 for UNC5B and NR2F2. Control GFP+ cells expressed UNC5B by P4 while remaining NR2F2 negative at both timepoints (Fig. 3g–j and Extended Data Fig. 8j–l). Mutant GFP+ cells were similar to controls at P4 but, by P6, demonstrated reduced UNC5B expression at the sprouting front and near arteries, along with ectopic NR2F2 expression (Fig. 3g–j and Extended Data Fig. 8j–n). These findings validate the scRNA-seq data and demonstrate that Pik3caH1047R progressively disrupts arterial differentiation in vivo.

To establish the temporal relationship between hyperproliferation and arterial differentiation defects, we examined the proliferative behaviour of Esm1-traced cells at P4 and P6. EdU incorporation showed that Esm1-traced cells normally retain proliferative capacity at P4, with proliferation beginning to diminish by P6 (Fig. 3k–m). Pik3caH1047R mutant Esm1-traced cells exhibited the same temporal pattern, although proliferation remained markedly higher at both timepoints, indicating that hyperproliferation precedes ectopic NR2F2 induction (Fig. 3k–m). The absence of a further increase in proliferation after NR2F2 induction at P6 argues against NR2F2 driving endothelial hyperproliferation.

It has been revealed that to test whether hyperproliferation accounts for defective arterial differentiation, we treated tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice with the CDK4 and CDK6 inhibitor palbociclib. Palbociclib partially reduced endothelial proliferation and vascular hyperplasia in tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas but did not restore arterial differentiation or suppress NR2F2 expression (Fig. 4a–h). Similar results were obtained with mitomycin C, which robustly inhibited endothelial expansion without restoring arterial incorporation or reducing NR2F2 expression in mutant GFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 9a–i). Consistently, palbociclib inhibited cell cycle progression in vitro but did not prevent Pik3caH1047R-driven NR2F2 upregulation (Fig. 4i–k and Extended Data Fig. 9j–m). Together, these findings show that suppressing proliferation does not prevent NR2F2 induction or restore arterial differentiation, supporting distinct effects of Pik3caH1047R signalling on proliferation and arterial specification. Consistent with this interpretation, scRNA-seq analysis revealed no association between Nr2f2 expression and cell cycle status in mutant GFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 10a).

It has been revealed that as Pik3caH1047R induces NR2F2 expression in pre-arterial endothelial cells, and NR2F2 suppresses arterial identity23,24,25,26, we hypothesized that NR2F2 mediates the arterial differentiation defect downstream of Pik3caH1047R. To test this hypothesis, we crossed the Nr2f2flox/flox allele with tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice (tip-cell-specific Nr2f2 deletion; hereafter, tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC mice) and optimized 4-OHT dosing to maximize recombination of both alleles (Fig. 5a). NR2F2 expression was efficiently reduced in tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC retinas (Extended Data Fig. 10b,c). Deletion of Nr2f2 alone neither impaired mobilization of Esm1-traced Nr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC-GFP+ cells into arteries nor altered vascular density (Fig. 5b–d and Extended Data Fig. 10d). Importantly, Nr2f2 deletion restored the ability of Pik3caH1047R cells to contribute to arteries (Fig. 5b,c), whereas endothelial hyperproliferation and vascular expansion remained essentially unchanged compared with tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice (Fig. 5d–f and Extended Data Fig. 10d).

We confirmed these findings using the complementary tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R clonal tracing model (Extended Data Fig. 11a–i). Whereas Cherry+ and Cherry+ Nr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC endothelial cells contributed similarly to arteries, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells were detected in 35% of arteries, compared with 10% for eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells (Extended Data Fig. 11c,e). Moreover, most eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells that reached arteries did not form lesions, whereas eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells consistently generated small arterial lesions (Extended Data Fig. 11c,f). Nevertheless, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells continued to overexpand within the capillary plexus (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i). Together, these findings demonstrate that NR2F2 mediates the PIK3CA-driven block in arterial differentiation but is dispensable for mutant cell hyperproliferation in non-arterial vessels.

To investigate how PIK3CAH1047R activation induces NR2F2 expression, we analysed endothelial cells in culture. Nr2f2 transcript levels increased within 24 h after 4-OHT-induced recombination and remained elevated thereafter (Extended Data Fig. 12a). NR2F2 protein levels increased by 72 h (Extended Data Fig. 12b–d). To test whether Nr2f2 induction depends on PI3K signalling, endothelial cells were treated with the PI3Kα-selective inhibitor alpelisib (BYL719). PI3Kα inhibition reduced Nr2f2 mRNA and protein levels in a dose-dependent manner, accompanied by reduced p-AKT levels (Extended Data Fig. 12e–h). Similarly, alpelisib reduced NR2F2 transcript and protein levels in patient-derived endothelial cells with activating PIK3CA mutations (Extended Data Fig. 12i,j).

To investigate the transcriptional mechanisms underlying NR2F2 induction, we focused on FOXO transcription factors, major downstream effectors of PI3K signalling7,32, with FOXO1 the predominant family member in endothelial cells33. PI3K–AKT signalling inhibits FOXO1 through phosphorylation-dependent nuclear exclusion7,32 and, consistent with this, FOXO1 was excluded from the nucleus in vascular lesions of Pik3caH1047R mutant mice (Extended Data Fig. 12k,l). We next examined whether FOXO1 directly regulates NR2F2. Analysis of published RNA-seq, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC–seq), FOXO1 chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) and H3K27ac ChIP–seq datasets from human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) expressing constitutively nuclear, PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3)34,35 revealed sustained repression of NR2F2 transcripts and protein, reduced chromatin accessibility at the NR2F2 locus and FOXO1 binding to a vein-specific NR2F2 enhancer (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12m–v). FOXO1(A3) increased occupancy at this enhancer while reducing H3K27 acetylation and chromatin accessibility, consistent with direct transcriptional repression (Extended Data Fig. 12p).

According to recent reports, conversely, endothelial deletion of Foxo1 markedly increased Nr2f2 transcript and protein levels (Fig. 5h,i). Finally, induction of PIK3CAH1047R in HUVECs increased NR2F2 expression, whereas the PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3) suppressed this response (Fig. 5j). Together, these findings establish FOXO1 as a transcriptional repressor of NR2F2 and define a PI3K–FOXO1–NR2F2 axis through which oncogenic PIK3CA disrupts arterial differentiation.

It has been revealed that using the vasculature as a model, we show that the consequences of PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial cell context. Depending on the differentiation state of the affected endothelial cell, the mutation promotes pathological proliferation, remains phenotypically silent or disrupts differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 13). This context-dependent model provides a mechanistic explanation for the marked predominance of capillary and venous lesions, and the rarity of arterial lesions, in PIK3CA-driven vascular disease. More broadly, it may also help to explain why PIK3CA-associated overgrowth preferentially affects mesoderm-derived tissues and suggests that similar principles probably apply to other pathogenic PIK3CA variants, which exhibit comparable lesion distributions in patients3.

Genetic lineage tracing revealed that endothelial cells expressing endogenous Pik3caH1047R persist in mature arteries without eliciting a detectable phenotype. Consistently, embryonic expression of Pik3caH1047R in Tie2+ cells does not give rise to arterial lesions32. This finding is unexpected given the broad endothelial expression of Pik3ca and the prominent role of PI3Kα signalling in all endothelial cells33. However, basal PI3K signalling is comparatively low in arteries and is not increased by endogenous Pik3caH1047R expression. By contrast, forced overexpression, enhances PI3K signalling and induces mild overgrowth in arterial endothelial cells that have not yet completed differentiation, suggesting that these cells require higher signalling levels to mount a pathological response than venous or capillary endothelial cells. Nevertheless, increased PI3K signalling does not induce overgrowth or NR2F2 expression in fully differentiated arteries. Likewise, reducing shear stress or Notch signalling, key pathways in the acquisition and maintenance of arterial identity30,34,35, does not restore responsiveness to Pik3caH1047R. These findings suggest that arterial endothelial cells possess multiple layers of protection that may also underlie their broader resistance to other mutations36. Future studies are needed to determine how microenvironmental cues, including extracellular matrix composition and mural cell interactions, contribute to this resistance.

We also find that PIK3CAH1047R disrupts arterial differentiation at early developmental stages. During angiogenesis, a subset of tip cells acquires a pre-arterial identity by expressing canonical arterial markers (such as CXCR4, UNC5B, HEY1 and DLL4)30,37,38 and migrates retrogradely into nascent arteries to support arterial expansion. Pik3caH1047R disrupts this transition by inducing an early hyperproliferation response followed by Nr2f2 upregulation and loss of arterial identity. Supporting a causal role for NR2F2, Nr2f2 deletion restored the ability of Pik3caH1047R tip cells to contribute to arteries, consistent with previous studies demonstrating that NR2F2 antagonizes pre-arterial specification26. More broadly, our findings align with evidence that PI3K signalling promotes venous specification39,40, suppresses arterial differentiation41 and favours a stemness state42. Similar effects have been reported in other tissues, where PIK3CAH1047R biases ageing oesophageal progenitor cells towards self-renewal and induces dedifferentiation during mammary tumorigenesis14,15. In parallel, we show that proliferation blockade in Pik3caH1047R-expressing pre-arterial cells limits lesion formation, but neither reduces NR2F2 expression nor restores arterial contribution of mutant cells. These findings indicate that impaired arterial differentiation cannot be explained solely by proliferative exclusion43,44. Conversely, NR2F2 depletion did not block lesion growth or endothelial proliferation, despite previous reports implicating NR2F2 in cell cycle regulation25,45. Together, these findings indicate that PIK3CAH1047R-driven endothelial proliferation and the NR2F2-mediated arterial differentiation defect are functionally separable downstream outputs.

Our findings identify a transcriptional mechanism linking PI3K activation to NR2F2 induction. Previous studies indicated that TIE2–PI3K signalling stabilizes NR2F2 protein during venous specification39 and that NR2F2 is elevated in PI3K-driven prostate tumours46. We show that PI3K signalling also promotes NR2F2 transcript and protein expression by inhibiting FOXO1. This is consistent with the established role of FOXO factors as nuclear effectors of PI3K signalling, including in PIK3CA-related vascular malformations47, and with the vascular overgrowth caused by endothelial FOXO1 loss48. Notably, FOXO1 has been reported to promote NR2F2 transcript and protein expression in pancreatic β cells49, whereas our data identify FOXO1 as a direct NR2F2 repressor in endothelial cells. Although the molecular basis of this difference remains to be determined, it is consistent with the context-dependent transcriptional activity of FOXO factors and NR2F2 regulation50,51 and may reflect differences in enhancer use and FOXO1 occupancy. Given that additional transcription factors regulate endothelial NR2F2 expression52,53,54, defining how they cooperate with or compete with FOXO1 will help to explain this context-dependent regulation.

It has been revealed that together, our findings show that the pathological consequences of oncogenic PIK3CA activation depend not only on signalling strength but also on developmental state and endothelial identity. Differentiated arterial cells resist pathological overgrowth, whereas pre-arterial cells undergo an NR2F2-mediated differentiation defect alongside increased proliferation. These functionally separable responses help to explain the vessel-type specificity of PIK3CA-driven vascular malformations.

It has been revealed that the in vivo experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines and legislation of the Catalan Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, Fisheries and Food (Catalonia, Spain), following protocols approved by the local animal experimentation ethics committee (CEEA) of the Institut Germans Trias i Pujol (IGTP) and local animal authorities of the State of Berlin (Landesamt für Gesundheit und Soziales Berlin). Mice were housed in individually ventilated cages under specific-pathogen-free conditions. All mice were crossed onto the C57BL/6J genetic background. Both male and female pups were used for retinal experiments.

The following mouse strains were used in this study. Pdgfb-creERT2-eGFP (pan-endothelial Cre line)55 mice were provided by M. Fruttiger. Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2 (pan-endothelial Cre line)56, Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 (arterial-endothelial Cre line)57 and Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 (tip-endothelial Cre line)58 mice were obtained from R. Adams. The R26-mTmG59 mice express membrane-targeted Tomato in the absence of Cre activity and this switches to membrane-targeted GFP expression after Cre activation, enabling cell lineage visualization and tracking. Pik3catm1.1Waph/+ mice, which harbour a Cre-inducible H1047R point mutation in the endogenous Pik3ca locus, were provided by W. Phillips60. In this allele, loxPsites flank exon 20, which is replaced after Cre recombination by a downstream version containing a CAT-to-AGG substitution at codon 1047. The two loxPsites are only 419 bp apart, making this region highly recombinogenic. Consistent with this, robust phenotypes are observed even at low doses of 4-OHT19. We occasionally observed vascular overgrowth in regions lacking GFP labelling, suggesting the presence of mutant cells in which the reporter allele had not recombined. Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R mice (hereafter iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R) overexpress the human PIK3CAH1047R cDNA along with H2B-eGFP-V5 (details are provided in the next section and Extended Data Fig. 5). The Nr2f2flox/flox mouse line61, provided by S. Y. Tsai, was used for conditional deletion of Nr2f2. The Foxo1flox/flox mouse line62 was used for conditional deletion of Foxo1. A list of all mouse lines and genotyping primer sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

To induce CreERT2 activity in pups, 4-OHT (Sigma-Aldrich, H7905) was dissolved in ethanol to prepare a 10 mg ml−1 solution. The stock solution was aliquoted and stored at −20 °C. Pups received intragastric injections in volumes adjusted to deliver the doses specified in the figures. To achieve the desired recombination pattern (such as sparse mosaic recombination, efficient recombination or recombination of multiple alleles), the 4-OHT dose was titrated for each CreERT2 line and experimental configuration (Supplementary Table 2).

To inhibit proliferation, pups received palbociclib (70 mg kg−1 in distilled H2O; Selleckchem S1116; intraperitoneal (i.p.), P3–P5) or mitomycin C (10 mg kg−1 in PBS, Sigma-Aldrich, M4287, i.p., P4–P5). To modulate blood flow and inhibit the Notch signalling pathway, pups received captopril (4.125 mg kg−1 in PBS; Sigma-Aldrich, C4042; i.p., P4–P5) or DAPT (100 mg kg−1 in DMSO/peanut oil; Calbiochem, 565770; subcutaneous, P4–P5). DAPT stock (10 mg ml−1) was prepared by dissolving 5 mg in 50 µl DMSO at 40 °C for 10 min and diluting in 450 µl peanut oil. To assess endothelial cell proliferation, pups were injected i.p. with 100 μg of EdU and euthanized 2 h later. EdU incorporated into the retina was detected using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 594 Imaging Kit (Invitrogen, C10339).

To generate the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R) mouse line, we introduced the DNA insert containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-humanPIK3CAH1047R gene by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated homologous-dependent repair, in the previously targeted iChr2-Mosaic mouse embryonic stem (ES) cell line31. To generate the donor construct of interest, we first obtained the HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence from the plasmid pBabe-puro-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R (Addgene, 12524) and cloned it into plasmid SO107 (Addgene, 99617)31, which contained the LoxP2-H2B-eGFP-V5-2A cassette. We then inserted the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R cassette into the donor vector JP6 (Addgene, 99627), which contains the hygromycin-resistance gene. This resulted in the generation of the donor vector NA453, containing the complete donor construct of interest (Extended Data Fig. 5). ES cells of the G4 genetic background63 were cultured in standard ES cell medium consisting of DMEM supplemented with GlutaMax (31966-047, Gibco), 15% FBS (tested for germline transmission), 1× non-essential amino acids (Hyclone, SH3023801), 0.1% β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich, M7522), 1× penicillin–streptomycin (Lonza, DE17-602E) and leukaemia inhibitory factor. ES cells were maintained on dishes coated with a feeder layer of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs). For each nucleofection, 2.5 × 106 ES cells were resuspended in 100 µl nucleofection solution containing 1.5 µg of circular px330 plasmid (NA505), encoding the guide RNA sequence (Guide3, GTTGCCTATGAGAGGCTAGAC), and 3.5 µg circular donor plasmid (NA453) containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence and the PGK-hygromycin resistance cassette (Extended Data Fig. 5). After nucleofection, 5 µl or 30 µl of the cell suspension was plated into separate wells on a six-well plate containing MEF feeder layers. Then, 7 days after hygromycin selection, 24 isolated ES cell colonies were picked for cryopreservation and subsequent screening. PCR with the flanking primers identified clones with correct homologous recombination and targeted insertion. After identifying correctly targeted ES cell clones, the functionality of the targeted allele was validated by transient transfection of a Cre-expressing plasmid. Positive clones were expanded and microinjected into C57BL/6J host blastocysts. Chimeric mice with a high degree of agouti coat colour were subsequently bred to achieve germline transmission of the targeted allele.

Mice were euthanized by decapitation, and their eyes were isolated and incubated on ice in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA; Sigma-Aldrich, 158127) in PBS for 1 h. Retinas were dissected and fixed for an additional 1 h in 4% PFA on ice, washed three times in PBS and incubated overnight at 4 °C in blocking buffer (1% BSA, 3% donkey serum and 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS) with gentle agitation. For NR2F2 staining, retinas were subjected to antigen retrieval by boiling for 20 min in 0.01 M citrate buffer (pH 6, Sigma-Aldrich, W305600) before permeabilization. Retinas were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with specific primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. In iFluMosaic-PIK3CA retinas, the antigen-retrieval step required for NR2F2 staining abolished the GFP signal and prevented detection with anti-GFP antibodies; therefore, the retinas were incubated overnight with anti-GFP antibodies before antigen retrieval. After washing three times in PBST (0.1% Tween-20 in PBS), the retinas were incubated for 30 min at room temperature in PBLEC buffer (1% Triton X-100, 1 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM MnCl2 in PBS (pH 6.8)). Secondary Alexa-Fluor-conjugated antibodies or isolectin GS-B4 (IB4) were incubated with retinas in PBLEC buffer for 2 h at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C. After three additional washes with PBST, retinas were flat-mounted onto microscope slides with Mowiol (Calbiochem, 475904), supplemented with the anti-fade reagent DABCO (1.4-diazabicyclo-(2.2.2)octane; Sigma-Aldrich, D27802) or Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, 0100-01). For FOXO1/ERG co-immunostaining, an additional blocking step was included because both primary antibodies were raised in the same species, thereby preventing cross-reactivity. After the incubation with the anti-FOXO1 antibody and its corresponding secondary antibody, retinas were incubated with AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragments donkey anti-rabbit IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711-006-152, 1:100) in PBS for 1 h at room temperature. The retinas were then washed, briefly fixed with 4% PFA, blocked again and incubated with the primary Alexa-Fluor-647-conjugated anti-ERG antibody. A list of all of the primary and secondary antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Sources indicate that mouse endothelial cells were isolated from the lungs of adult mice (both female and male) aged 3 to 6 weeks. Under sterile conditions, lungs were minced and digested in 4 U ml−1 dispase II (Roche, 04942078001) in Hanks’ balanced salt solution (Gibco, 14170-112) for 1 h at 37 °C with constant agitation. Tissue was further dissociated by pipetting to obtain a single-cell suspension, and digestion was stopped with Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Corning, 10-013-CV) supplemented with 10% FBS (Biowest, S1810-500) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, 15140-122). Cells were resuspended in PBS and incubated for 30 min at room temperature with rat anti-CD144 (Cdh5; BD Biosciences, 55289) antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads (Invitrogen, 11035). CD144+ cells were washed in PBS containing 0.5% BSA and sorted by magnetic separation. CD144+ cells were plated on 0.5% gelatine-coated 12-well plates (Sigma-Aldrich, G1890) and cultured in complete DMEM/F12 (PromoCell, C-30140) supplemented with 20% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and two vials of endothelial cell growth supplement/heparin (ECGF/H; PromoCell, C-30120). Once confluent, a second selection with CD144-antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads was performed for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were trypsinized, magnet-sorted, resuspended in F12 complete medium and cultured in a six-well format. Cells were maintained at 37 °C under a 5% CO2 atmosphere and used for experiments up to passage 5. Primary cells were not tested for mycoplasma contamination. Mouse endothelial cells used in Fig. 5i,j were isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2Foxo1flox/flox lungs as described previously64.

Subconfluent HUVECs were transduced with custom-made adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs) to overexpress constitutively nuclear human FOXO1 (FOXO1A3-Flag) or control (CMV-null) adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs, 1300). For adenoviral transductions, HUVECs were incubated in EBM medium (Lonza, CC-3121) containing 0.1% (v/v) BSA (Sigma-Aldrich, 1595) for 4 h and transduced with the respective viruses for an additional 4 h in the presence of 8 µg ml−1 polybrene (Santa Cruz, sc-134220). HUVECs were then washed five times with Hank’s balanced salt solution (Gibco, 14175095) and cultured for the indicated times in EBM basal medium supplemented with 10% FBS and EGM SingleQuots.

Gene-specific gRNA sequences to target the NR2F2-1345 enhancer were designed using CHOPCHOP66. For each target gene, we used three independent gRNAs and co-transfected them with packaging vectors for lentivirus production. After transduction, puromycin was used to select a pool of CRISPR–Cas9-mediated mutant HUVECs. The knockout efficiency was confirmed by PCR analysis of gDNA isolated from transduced cells. Single guide RNA sequences and genotyping primers are provided in Supplementary Table 4.

Sources indicate that cells were washed with warm 1% PBS containing Mg2+ and Ca2+ (Gibco, 14080-055), fixed for 15 min in 4% PFA and washed again with warm PBS. For staining, cells were permeabilized for 5 min with 0.4% Triton X-100 in PBS, followed by a 1 h incubation in blocking buffer (2% BSA in PBS). After washing with PBS, cells were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. Subsequently, secondary AlexaFluor-conjugated antibodies were diluted in blocking buffer and added to the cells for a 1 h incubation at room temperature.
